extracted.intended_audience: federal agency rulemaking officials, the eRulemaking Project Management Office, and policymakers involved in notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Recommendations for agencies and the eRulemaking PMO on designing and administering the public comment portion of notice-and-comment rulemaking to promote public participation and improve the usefulness of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on types of effective comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking Project Management Office should consider publishing a document explaining what types of comments are most beneficial and listing best practices for parties submitting comments. Individual agencies may publish supplements to the common document describing the qualities of effective comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once developed, these documents should be made publicly available by posting on the agency website, Regulations.gov, and any other venue that will promote widespread availability of the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of comment periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should set comment periods that consider the competing interests of promoting optimal public participation while ensuring that the rulemaking is conducted efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a general matter, for "[s]ignificant regulatory action[s]" as defined in Executive Order 12,866, agencies should use a comment period of at least 60 days. For all other rulemakings, they should generally use a comment period of at least 30 days. When agencies, in appropriate circumstances, set shorter comment periods, they are encouraged to provide an appropriate explanation for doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posting comments to the Internet promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt stated policies of posting public comments to the Internet within a specified period after submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should post all electronically submitted comments on the Internet and should also scan and post all comments submitted in paper format. (Recommend posting on Regulations.gov and timely posting regardless of submission method.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Policies on anonymous comments
rubrics_metrics.description: The eRulemaking Project Management Office and individual agencies should establish and publish policies regarding the submission of anonymous comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should make clear whether anonymous comments are permitted, and explain the treatment and posting of anonymous or confidential submissions in publicly available policy statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policies on late comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should adopt and publish policies on late comments and should apply those policies consistently within each rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should determine whether or not they will accept late submissions in a given rulemaking and should announce the policy both in publicly accessible forums (e.g., the agency’s website, Regulations.gov) and in individual Federal Register notices including requests for comments. The agency may make clear that late comments are disfavored and will only be considered to the extent practicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of reply comment periods and other opportunities for input on submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriate, agencies should make use of reply comment periods or other opportunities for receiving public input on submitted comments, after all comments have been posted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An opportunity for public input on submitted comments can entail a reply period for written comments on submitted comments, an oral hearing, or some other means for input on comments received. Agencies should consider these mechanisms when comments or responses present new issues or conflicts in data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring staleness of the rulemaking record and use of supplemental notices
rubrics_metrics.description: Although agencies should not automatically deem rulemaking comments to have become stale after any fixed period of time, agencies should closely monitor their rulemaking dockets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an agency believes the circumstances surrounding the rulemaking have materially changed or the rulemaking record has otherwise become stale, it should consider using available mechanisms such as supplemental notices of proposed rulemaking to refresh the rulemaking record.
